transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. I came in because... well, at the register at work, I keep getting stuck doing things that just don’t fit the moment. I'm a cashier, and I'll catch myself tapping the scanner in this pattern, or I'll just completely freeze with my hand hovering right over the cash drawer while the customer is waiting. 

Customers buy the strangest combinations of things, you know. Just yesterday a lady bought three cans of shoe polish and a single cucumber. It made me think about this cucumber salad I used to make back when I was getting my bachelor's degree. Just cucumbers, vinegar, and onions. My roommate absolutely hated the smell of the vinegar. He was from Ohio, always talked about how cold the winters were there compared to here. I've never been to Ohio myself, but I imagine it's pretty flat. 

But, um... anyway, what was I saying? Right, the register. Yeah, the freezing and the tapping... my manager saw it happen again, and it actually got me written up last week. So I guess that's why I'm here.
When you tap the scanner in that pattern, do you feel like you have to do it, or does it just happen without you really choosing to do it?

I'm not really sure, honestly. I don't know if I'm choosing it or... if it just happens. I just look down and my hand is doing it. 

The scanner has this little red laser line, you know? And it blinks if you don't scan something for a few minutes. It kind of reminds me of this broken traffic light near my old apartment, back right after I finished my degree. It was stuck on blinking red for almost a whole month. Nobody ever knew whose turn it was to go, so people would just inch forward into the intersection. I actually saw a garbage truck back right into a blue mailbox there once. The mail carrier was so mad, he was waving his little package scanner around at the driver. His scanner looked a lot like the ones we use at the store, just more heavy-duty, I guess. They have to be, being outside in the weather all day. The rain gets pretty bad here in the spring... 

But, wait, what did you ask me? Oh, about having to tap it. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't really noticed a feeling with it.

Before you start tapping the scanner or freezing up, do you ever have thoughts or worries that make you feel like you need to do these things? Or do the thoughts come after you've already started doing them?

I don't really have any thoughts or worries before it happens. It's just... I'm standing there, and then I'm doing it. Or not doing anything, I guess, when I freeze. 

It's funny you mention worrying, though, because my manager, Gary, is a huge worrier. He's always pacing around the break room, fretting about the inventory numbers or if the delivery truck is going to be late. The truck driver is this guy named Dale, and he always wears these really bright neon green shirts. He told me once he buys them in bulk online because he hates doing laundry. I get that, laundry is such a chore. Especially folding fitted sheets. I watched a video once on how to fold them perfectly into a square, but I can never get the corners to line up right. They always just end up in a crumpled ball in my linen closet. I have this one blue sheet set from college that's almost completely worn through in the middle... 

But, um, thoughts before I freeze? No, no thoughts like that. It just happens.

When you're at the register, do you ever have thoughts that feel like they just pop into your head—thoughts that feel unwanted or that you wish you could get rid of—even if you can't quite remember them right now?

No, I don't think so. Unwanted thoughts... I don't really get those. My head is pretty quiet most of the time when I'm working. 

Well, except for the music they play over the store speakers. It's always this mix of, like, soft rock from the eighties and these weirdly upbeat instrumental covers of modern pop songs. It gets stuck in your head, you know? The other day they played this instrumental version of a song that sounded exactly like the theme song to this old sitcom I used to watch with my dad when I was a kid. We used to sit in the living room, and he had this big, ugly brown recliner that he refused to get rid of, even when the springs started poking through the fabric. My mom hated that chair. She tried to throw a blanket over it, this knitted afghan she got at a craft fair, but it always slipped off because the fabric on the chair was so worn down and slick. She loved craft fairs, though. Always came home with little wooden birdhouses or homemade soaps that smelled like lavender... 

But, uh, unwanted thoughts popping in? No, I don't have anything like that. Just the store music, really.

Has anyone ever told you that the way you talk or think seems confusing or hard to follow? Or have you noticed that your thoughts seem to jump around a lot, even when you're trying to focus on something?

Confusing? I don't... I don't think anyone's said that to me. I mean, my sister gets annoyed with me sometimes, but she's always been impatient. She's a real estate agent, so she's always rushing around, talking a mile a minute on her phone. She has this headset thing she wears so she can drive and talk at the same time. She drives a silver Honda CR-V, the one with the sunroof. I rode in it once when she took me to get my eyes checked. The optometrist was this really tall guy with a bowtie. He had all these framed pictures of lighthouses in his office. I guess he really liked lighthouses. I visited one once, in Maine, on a road trip right after college. The stairs going up were so narrow and spiraled, it made me dizzy just looking down. The view from the top was incredible, though. You could see the ocean for miles, just this deep, dark blue... 

But, what were you asking? Oh, if my thoughts jump around. I don't really notice that. I just think about whatever comes to mind, I guess.
When you're not at work, do you ever find yourself thinking about things repeatedly—like thoughts you can't seem to stop or get out of your head—even though you don't want to be thinking about them?

Repeated thoughts? No, not really. I mean, I think about things a normal amount. Like, when I'm home, I might think about my garden, but I *want* to think about that, you know? It's not like I can't stop or anything. I've just been trying to get these tomato plants to take off, but the soil in my backyard is so full of clay. 

I had to go down to the hardware store last weekend to buy this special compost mix to try and break it up. The guy working in the garden center was really helpful, actually. He had this thick mustache, kind of looked exactly like Tom Selleck. My dad used to watch Magnum P.I. all the time when I was growing up. We had this heavy old Zenith television set with the dials on the front, and you actually had to get up off the couch to change the channel. Sometimes the antenna would get fuzzy and you'd have to put tin foil on the tips of the rabbit ears just to get a clear picture. I remember burning my hand on the back of that TV once because the glass tubes inside got so hot... 

But, um, what were you asking? Thoughts I can't get out of my head? No, I don't really have anything like that bother me.
Have you ever experienced times when things didn't seem real, or when you saw or heard things that other people around you couldn't see or hear?

Hear things? Well, yeah, I guess so. Most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking, just off to the side of me. Sometimes they're calling my name from the stockroom, or saying I rang something up wrong. Which is frustrating because those registers are ancient. The buttons stick all the time. It's one of those old gray machines, and the screen has this weird flicker if you stare at it too long. 

My buddy Dave in college had a computer monitor that flickered exactly like that. We were roommates sophomore year, lived in this cramped dorm on the fourth floor. There was no elevator, so moving in was a total nightmare. We had to carry this heavy mini-fridge up all those stairs, and Dave actually slipped and almost dropped the whole thing right on my foot. He was always kind of clumsy like that. I remember he spilled black coffee on his keyboard twice in one semester, just completely ruined it. Had to write his final paper in the library computer lab... 

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, the talking. I'll hear them saying I messed up a ring-up or calling for me, but when I turn around, there’s nobody there. And no one else around me ever hears it.

When you hear those voices calling your name or saying you made a mistake at the register, do they sound like they're coming from an actual external source—like real people speaking to you—or does it feel more like thoughts in your own head?

External source? I don't know... I'm really not sure. I haven't paid that much attention to exactly where they're coming from, to be honest. They just sound like... well, like people talking. Like the customers that come through my lane. 

Speaking of customers, this one lady came through yesterday with, I kid you not, forty cans of that Fancy Feast cat food. The chicken pate kind. My aunt Martha used to have a cat that would only eat the pate. He was this massive orange tabby named Marmalade. Meanest cat you ever met, honestly. He'd swipe at your ankles if you even walked past the refrigerator. She had to keep his food on top of this old chest freezer out in the garage so her dog wouldn't get into it. That freezer was older than I am, I swear. It had this thick rubber seal that was peeling off, and it hummed so loud you could hear it all the way from the driveway. One summer the compressor finally went out while she was visiting my cousin in Ohio, and all her frozen Omaha Steaks completely thawed out and ruined. It stunk up the whole garage for a month, she had to hire a guy to come haul the whole thing to the dump... 

But, um, anyway, what were you asking? If they're in my head? I really couldn't tell you. I just hear them when I'm trying to work.

When you're telling someone a story or explaining something, do people ever tell you that they have trouble following what you're saying, or that you're jumping between topics too much? Or do you ever notice that yourself—like you start talking about one thing and end up somewhere completely different?

Trouble following me? No, I don't think so. I mean, nobody's ever said anything to me about it. I just talk like regular. Like when I'm chatting with the regulars at the store, you know? 

There's this one guy, Mr. Henderson, he comes in every Tuesday morning to buy the crossword puzzle book and a pack of spearmint gum. He always wears this bright yellow windbreaker, even when it's eighty degrees out. Said he got it on a fishing trip up in Michigan back in the nineties. My uncle went fishing in Michigan once, caught a walleye the size of his leg. He had it stuffed and mounted over his fireplace. The glass eyes on that thing always creeped me out when I was a kid. It felt like it was watching you no matter where you sat in the living room. His living room had this really awful shag carpet, too—like, puke green. You'd lose change in it for weeks. I remember dropping a quarter in there and finding a whole handful of pennies and a stale Cheeto instead. We used to eat those puffy Cheetos all the time while watching cartoons on Saturday mornings...

But, um, what was the question? Jumping between topics? No, I don't really notice anything like that. I just tell stories how they happen.
When you talk to your sister or your coworkers, do they ever seem confused or frustrated, or do they ask you to repeat yourself or get back to the main point?

Confused? I mean, my sister gets frustrated with me sometimes, sure. But she's just like that. She's always been kind of high-strung, you know? Even when we were kids. 

She used to have this obsession with keeping her room perfectly clean. Like, vacuum lines in the carpet kind of clean. Our mom bought her this little toy vacuum for her fifth birthday, and she'd push it around for hours. It was bright pink with these little plastic beads inside that popped when you rolled it. I stepped on it once in the hallway and cracked the wheel off. Man, she threw an absolute fit. Screamed so loud the neighbors probably thought someone was getting murdered. Those neighbors were really strange, actually. The Millers. They had this huge garden in their backyard, but they only grew zucchini. Just rows and rows of giant zucchini. One time Mr. Miller gave us a grocery bag full of them, and my mom tried to make zucchini bread for like a month straight to use it all up. I still can't stand the smell of cinnamon and baked squash. Makes me gag just thinking about it. She used to bake it in these heavy glass loaf pans that were impossible to scrub clean...

But, uh, wait, what were you saying? Do they ask me to get back to the point? No, not really. My coworkers just kind of nod mostly. We're all just trying to get through the shift.
Has a boss, coworker, or family member ever actually told you directly that your speech is hard to follow—like, they've said something to you about it, not just seemed annoyed?

Directly? No, nobody's ever come right out and said those words to me. My manager, Gary, he doesn't really say much of anything to us unless it's about our scan rates. He's obsessed with how fast we ring people up. 

He stands up at the front podium with this little metal clipboard—you know, the kind that opens up so you can keep extra papers inside? My dad had one of those when he worked construction. He used to keep all his invoices and sketches in it. He built this massive deck on the back of our house when I was in high school. Took him all summer because he insisted on using this specific kind of cedar wood that he had to drive two hours to get from some specialty lumber yard out in the county. He drove this beat-up old Ford pickup truck, and the heater was stuck on full blast, so if you rode with him in July, you were just sweating buckets the whole time. We had to roll all the windows down, and the wind would whip around so loud you couldn't even hear the radio. He mostly listened to classic rock anyway, lots of Bob Seger. We had this one cassette tape that got stuck in the player, so it just looped the same eight songs for like three years straight...

But, um... wait, did Gary say something? No, Gary just cares about how fast we scan the cans. He's never said anything about how I talk. None of them have.

When you're telling a story like you just did about your dad's truck, do you feel like you're following a logical path in your own mind—like each thought connects to the next one in a way that makes sense to you—even if other people might not see the connection?

Makes sense to me? Yeah, of course it does. It all just links right up in my head. One thing just reminds me of the next, like... like dominoes falling, you know? Or like when you're trying to follow one specific wire in that huge tangle of cords behind the television set. I was actually trying to sort mine out last week because my cable box kept cutting out right in the middle of Jeopardy. I really miss Alex Trebek. Ken Jennings is alright, I guess, but he's just not the same. My buddy Mark and I used to watch Jeopardy every single day in the breakroom back when I worked at the distribution center in my thirties. 

Mark always brought these massive tuna salad sandwiches that just completely stunk up the whole room. I don't know why people think it's acceptable to eat fish in a small enclosed space like that. We only had this one tiny little microwave, and somebody exploded a pepperoni Hot Pocket in it and just left the mess. The cheese was baked onto the ceiling of the thing for months. It smelled like burnt oregano every time you tried to heat up a cup of water for tea. I usually drink Earl Grey, but sometimes I like peppermint if my stomach is acting up. Peppermint is supposed to be really good for digestion. My grandmother used to grow it in her backyard right next to the tomatoes...

Wait, what were we talking about? Do the thoughts connect? Yeah, I mean, they connect fine for me. I'm just explaining things how they happen.
When you were a kid in school, did your teachers ever mention anything about how you organized your thoughts or the way you spoke and explained things to other kids?

Teachers? No, I don't remember them ever saying anything about that. Mostly they just complained about my handwriting. I had terrible cursive. Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, she used to make me stay inside during recess to practice my capital letters. 

We had to use those really thick yellow pencils, you know the ones? With the giant pink erasers that didn't actually erase anything, they just left these huge pink smears all over the paper and ripped the page if you pressed too hard. I used to chew on the metal part holding the eraser. My dentist, Dr. Aris, gave my mom a whole lecture about it once because he said it was wearing down my enamel. His office was right above this old bakery downtown. You could smell fresh sourdough bread while you were sitting in the dentist's chair getting your teeth scraped. It was a really weird combination of smells, the minty fluoride paste and the baking yeast. That bakery shut down a few years ago, actually. It got replaced by a mattress store. I really don't understand how those mattress stores stay in business, they're always completely empty every time you walk by. I bought my current mattress from a guy on Craigslist a few years back, which was probably a mistake because the springs squeak really loud every time I roll over, and it takes me forever to get to sleep anyway...

Wait, what did you ask me? Did the teachers say something? No, just the handwriting thing. I don't remember them ever saying anything about how I talked to the other kids.

When you listen to yourself talking, or when you think back on a conversation you just had, do you ever realize that you went way off track or talked about a bunch of unrelated things, even though it all seemed connected while you were saying it?

Do I realize it? I don't know, maybe sometimes? I mean, I'm just talking. It's just normal conversation to me. Like when I talk to my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins. She's always out on her porch watering those geraniums. She's got these huge terracotta pots that she painted blue. 

Actually, she painted her whole front door blue last spring. Said it was supposed to bring good luck or keep away bad spirits or something. I think she read it in a magazine. She gets all those home and garden magazines delivered every Tuesday. The mail carrier, Dave, he always stops to chat with her for like twenty minutes. Dave's a nice guy, he wears those little blue shorts even when it's like forty degrees outside. I asked him about it once, and he said his legs just don't get cold. My legs are always cold. I have to wear thermal socks from October all the way through April. I buy them in bulk from this catalog my sister sends me for my birthday every year. My sister lives out in Oregon now, near Portland. It rains there constantly, I don't know how she stands it. I need the sun, you know? If it's cloudy for more than three days in a row, my joints start aching. Mostly my left knee. I twisted it pretty bad playing softball in a company league back in the nineties...

But, um... wait, do I notice going off track? No, not really. I just talk about what comes to mind, you know? It's just how I talk.
Has anyone ever actually stopped you mid-conversation and said something like 'I don't understand what you're saying' or 'I'm lost' or asked you to explain what you mean?

People stopping me? Um... no, not really. I mean, nobody usually stops me right in the middle of talking. People are mostly pretty polite, you know? Like at the grocery store where I work, the customers just want to get through the line. They're always in such a rush. 

Especially on Sundays right after church gets out, the whole place is just packed with people buying roasts and potatoes. It's crazy how many people still do a big Sunday dinner. My mom used to make a pot roast every single Sunday, with the carrots and the little pearl onions. She had this heavy cast iron Dutch oven that weighed a ton. I think my brother took it when she passed away. He lives out in Denver now, works for some tech company. He's always flying all over the place for conferences. I don't know how he deals with all the airport security, taking your shoes off and unpacking your laptop. I haven't been on a plane since... gosh, maybe 2005? I went to Florida for a buddy's wedding. It was so humid down there, my hair just wouldn't stay flat. And the bugs, they have these giant palmetto bugs that look like cockroaches on steroids...

But no, nobody really says they're lost when I'm talking. I think I'm pretty clear. They usually just nod and say 'have a good day' when I hand them their receipt.

I want to circle back to something. When you're talking to someone—like your sister or a coworker—and you finish telling them a whole story, do they ever seem confused about what you were trying to say, or do they ever ask you clarifying questions about what you meant?

Confused? No, I don't think so. My sister, she usually just listens. We talk on the phone every Sunday evening. She calls me right after she finishes watching that baking show she likes. The one with the British people in the big white tent. She's obsessed with it. 

She actually tried to make one of those fancy cakes they do on the show for her husband's birthday last month. A genoise sponge, I think she called it. But her oven runs hot, so the edges got all crispy and the middle sank in. She ended up just covering the whole thing in store-bought frosting and calling it a day. Frosting fixes everything, really. I used to love those little tubs of chocolate frosting when I was a kid. Sometimes I'd just eat it with a spoon right out of the fridge when my mom wasn't looking. The cold frosting was the best. It got all dense and fudgy. I can't eat stuff like that anymore, though. Gives me terrible heartburn. I have to keep a bottle of antacids in my locker at work now. The store brand ones, they're just as good as the name brand, and they're like half the price. I don't get why people pay extra for the fancy label when the ingredients are exactly the same. You just have to read the back of the bottle. 

But anyway, no, my sister doesn't get confused. We just chat about her baking or whatever. And my coworkers, they're usually just complaining about the schedule or the managers, so they don't really ask questions about what I'm saying. They just want to vent.

If I played back a recording of one of our conversations right now and you listened to it, would you be able to hear how you jump from topic to topic—like from talking about your dad's truck to talking about Jeopardy to talking about your grandmother's garden—or would it all still sound connected to you?

A recording? Um... I don't know, I think it would just sound like me talking. It would all make sense to me, you know? Because one thing just naturally leads to the next. 

But speaking of recordings, I used to have this old dual-deck cassette player back when I was getting my degree. You know, to make mixtapes. I had hundreds of them stacked up in these little wooden crates from the craft store. I used to record songs right off the radio. You had to sit there with your finger just hovering over the record button, waiting for the DJ to stop talking. The worst was when they talked right over the intro of the song. I was trying to get this one Phil Collins song once, because of that famous drum solo. My buddy Mark had this huge drum kit in his basement back then. We used to go down there and he'd just bang on those things for hours. His mom was an absolute saint for putting up with all that noise. She used to make us these incredible grilled cheese sandwiches with tomato soup. The secret, she told me, was putting a little bit of mayonnaise on the outside of the bread instead of butter before you put it in the pan. It makes it so much crispier. I actually still make them exactly that way. I had one for lunch yesterday before my shift at the register, but I burned the roof of my mouth on the soup. It's still a little tender right now, actually... 

But yeah, if you played a tape of me, I think it would just sound like a regular conversation. Everything connects if you just listen to it.

If I told you that in our conversation today you've jumped from talking about your job at the register to your dad's truck, to Jeopardy, to your grandmother's garden, to cassette tapes—and that those topics don't really connect to each other—would you be able to see that, or would it still seem like everything was connected to you?

I mean... if you told me they didn't connect, I guess I'd just have to disagree with you. Because to me, it all seems perfectly connected. You can't really talk about one thing without the other coming up, you know? 

Like Jeopardy. You mentioned Jeopardy. That just naturally makes me think of the evening routine, because it's always on right after the local news. You sit down with your dinner, the news is wrapping up with the weather, and then that theme song starts playing. I used to watch the weather just to see what kind of tie the meteorologist was wearing. We had this guy on channel 4, Stan something, and he wore the most ridiculous ties. One had little rubber ducks all over it, another had golf clubs. I always wondered where he found them all. Probably that novelty shop that used to be down at the mall. 

The mall used to be so great back in the day. They had this massive fountain right in the center court, and the water smelled a little bit like chlorine, like a swimming pool. People would throw pennies in and make wishes. I threw a lot of pennies in there wishing for a blue Schwinn bicycle. The kind with the silver bell. I ended up getting a red Huffy from a garage sale instead, but it was alright. The chain used to slip off if you pedaled too fast, so my hands were always covered in black grease from putting it back on the gears. My mom hated that, she was always scrubbing my hands with that gritty orange soap mechanics use... 

But yeah, I don't really get what you mean about jumping around. Everything just connects to the next thing. It's just how a normal conversation flows, isn't it?

When you were talking about your dad's truck and then suddenly switched to talking about Jeopardy and Alex Trebek, can you explain to me right now how those two topics are actually connected to each other? What's the link between them?

Well, the truck... my dad's truck was this old Ford, right? And the radio in it only picked up AM stations clearly. So we'd be driving, and he'd always have it tuned to this news radio station. It was just talking, all the time. Just voices. And the announcer on that station, he had this really deep, smooth voice. Kind of like Alex Trebek's voice. You know how Alex Trebek always sounded so calm and in control, no matter what the contestants did? Even when they wagered everything on a Daily Double and got it completely wrong, he just had that steady voice. 

I always thought I'd be good on Jeopardy, actually. I know a lot of random trivia. Mostly history stuff. I read this whole book once about the history of the postal service. It's fascinating, really. The Pony Express only lasted for like 18 months, which is crazy when you think about how famous it is. Everyone knows about the Pony Express, but it was just a blip in time. The guys who rode for them had to be really small and lightweight so the horses could go faster. I think there was even an ad that said "orphans preferred," which is pretty grim if you think about it. But back then, I guess you did what you had to do for work. Just like now, really. Standing at the register all day isn't exactly glamorous, but it pays the bills. Mostly. I had to get my shoes resoled last week because I wore right through the heel standing on that hard floor. The cobbler charged me forty bucks. Forty bucks! I could have almost bought a new pair for that. But they're comfortable, you know? Once you break a pair of shoes in, you don't want to just throw them away. 

But yeah, the truck radio and Alex Trebek's voice, that's the connection. It makes perfect sense to me.

When I point out that talking about your dad's truck and then Alex Trebek doesn't really have a clear connection—even though you just explained the radio voice link—does it feel like I'm right and you just didn't notice it before, or does it still feel to you like those things are genuinely connected in a way that makes sense?

I mean, it still feels genuinely connected to me. Because that's just how my brain works, right? The radio voice makes me think of Trebek, and Trebek makes me think of the show. It's like a chain. You pull one link, the next one comes with it. 

Speaking of chains, I had to buy a new one for my dog last year. Well, he's not really my dog, he's my neighbor's dog, this big golden retriever named Buster. But he basically lives in my yard. He dug a hole right under the fence near the rhododendrons. Those bushes have been there since I bought the house in '98. I got a really good rate on the mortgage back then, before all the housing market stuff went crazy. The guy at the bank had this massive fish tank in his office. Saltwater, too, which is really hard to maintain. He had these little clownfish swimming around the anemones. It takes a lot of dedication to keep the pH levels right in those tanks. You have to test the water almost every day with these little chemical drops that turn the water pink or blue depending on the acidity. Reminds me of high school chemistry class. Mr. Henderson was our teacher, and he used to wear these thick safety goggles that always fogged up when he talked... 

So, yeah, I don't really see what you mean. The truck and Alex Trebek are totally connected. It's just how one thought leads to the next.
